title: Gargi's two questions
word: reading the Isha in the original
hook: Gargi stands up twice, and gets an answer made of nots
carry: nirguna and saguna: beyond form, and with a face
tomorrow: can twelve years of study leave you missing the one thing?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shankara in the alley, and the same self in every being; don't shrink away. Today, how do you even describe what's in every being? One woman asked, twice.
screen: `THE SAME SELF IN EVERY BEING.` · `NOW: HOW DO YOU DESCRIBE IT?`

segments.voice: King Janaka of Videha calls a great debate and sets out a thousand cows, gold tied to their horns, for the wisest one there. The sage Yajnavalkya tells his student: drive them home. The other scholars line up to stop him. One of them is a woman, Gargi Vachaknavi. She asks what everything is woven on, and what that is woven on, higher and higher, until he warns her: Gargi, don't ask too far. She sits down. Later she stands up again. Like a warrior stringing a bow with two arrows, she says, I have two questions.
screen: `A THOUSAND COWS, GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.` → `GARGI: DON'T ASK TOO FAR.` → `SHE STANDS UP AGAIN. TWO ARROWS.`

segments.voice: Her question: what is everything woven on, past, present, future, even space? Yajnavalkya answers with a list of nots. The Imperishable is not coarse, not fine, not short, not long, without shadow, without darkness, without air, without space. And then he turns: it is never seen, but it is the seer. Never heard, but it is the hearer. Gargi tells the room: none of you will beat him. Now read Isha eight, and watch the same move. Sa paryagat: he has gone everywhere. Then the nots: akayam, bodiless. Avranam, woundless. Asnaviram, without sinews. A short a at the front works like un-. And halfway through, the turn: kavir manishi. A poet, a thinker, who set all things in order. That's the puzzle, and it holds one of Hinduism's great teachings. God, Brahman, can be spoken of two ways. Nirguna: without qualities, beyond every picture, so the honest words are neti neti, not this, not this. And saguna: with qualities, a poet, a friend, a face you can garland. Hindus don't have to pick one. That's why the same Nani who says God has no form wakes Krishna with a bell every morning, bathes him and dresses him. In the reading many teachers give, the form isn't a mistake about the formless. It's the formless, turned toward us, close enough to love.
screen: `NOT COARSE, NOT FINE: THE SEER.` · `ISHA EIGHT: THE SAME NOTS.` · `NIRGUNA AND SAGUNA.` · `THE FORMLESS, TURNED TOWARD US.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes. Let a picture of God come up, any you've seen: a blue Krishna, a lamp, a wide sky. On each out-breath let one go: not this, not this. Then, if you pray, open your eyes to one image or murti you love and greet it. If you don't pray, open them to one thing you love. Both moves are the practice.
Reading the Isha in the original, verse eight: akayam, bodiless, and then kavi, a poet. Beyond every form, and close enough to name.
screen: `READING THE ISHA IN THE ORIGINAL — today's word`.

segments.voice: The line to keep: nirguna and saguna, beyond form, and with a face. Gargi got both in one answer. Rest easy.

screen: `DAY 1493 COUNTS.` → `NIRGUNA AND SAGUNA: BEYOND FORM, AND WITH A FACE.` → `TOMORROW: TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY, AND ONE THING MISSING?`

howItsDone: Hindu teachers describe two ways of speaking of the ultimate: by what it is not (neti neti, nirguna) and by what it is (saguna, with a form to love and serve); many families who say God has no form still wake, bathe and dress a murti every morning.

fork.setup: a friend visiting a temple with you whispers: 'i thought hindus said god is beyond all forms. why all the statues?' what's the fairest answer?
options: god is beyond form, nirguna, and also takes form for us, saguna; hindus hold both.
the statues are the whole thing; the beyond-form talk is just philosophy.
the Isha settles it: only the formless is real, so the statues are a mistake.
fork.reveal: Yajnavalkya's nots and Isha 8's turn to a poet say the same thing: beyond every picture, and close enough to garland.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: neti neti, 'not this, not this', the Brihadaranyaka's way of speaking of Brahman by what it is not.

trapdoor: what you thought: an abstract list of what God isn't.
what it means: a portrait drawn in nots, then a turn to a poet; Hindus speak of God as nirguna and saguna both.

what a scholar hears: the privative a- builds akayam, avranam, asnaviram in neuter forms while sa, kavih and manishi are masculine; Yajnavalkya's answer to Gargi (Brihadaranyaka 3.8) makes the same turn from nots to 'the seer'.
recall: the same self in every being

chat.says: Sam asked why Nani bathes and dresses her Krishna statue if hindus say god has no form. what do i say??
options: both are hindu: god beyond every form, and god with a face to love. the Isha says both in one verse.
tell him the statue is just decoration; real hindus only believe in the formless.
tell him the form is all there is; 'no form' is a modern idea.
chat.meaning: Yajnavalkya answered Gargi with nots and then called the Imperishable the seer; Isha 8 paints in nots and then turns to a poet. Nirguna and saguna together are why Nani's morning puja fits 'God has no form'.

tie.story: Yajnavalkya answered Gargi with a string of nots and then called the Imperishable the seer; Isha 8 makes the same turn, from nots to a poet.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Sam that Nani's morning puja to Krishna and 'God has no form' are two halves of one Hindu teaching.
tie.you: which do you reach for first, the face or the beyond?

Gargi.meaning: Gargi Vachaknavi, a woman sage who questions Yajnavalkya

Yajnavalkya.meaning: a sage of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad

nirguna.meaning: without qualities; God beyond every picture

saguna.meaning: with qualities; God with a form to love

akayam.meaning: without a body; kaya is body

kavir.meaning: a poet, a seer (kavih before a sound)

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 8, first line (sa paryagac chukram akayam avranam asnaviram shuddham apapaviddham)
Isha Upanishad 8, second line (kavir manishi paribhuh svayambhuh; set things in order for endless years)

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.1 (Janaka's debate and the thousand cows), 3.6 (Gargi's first questions; 'don't ask too far'), 3.8 (Gargi's two questions like two arrows; the Imperishable described by nots, then 'never seen, but the seer'; Gargi: none of you will defeat him)

notes: Year one, day 236, listed verse eight's qualities briefly; this day reads the privative a-, the compound apapaviddham, and the shift between neuter (shukram, akayam…) and masculine (sa, kavih, manishi…) forms. The spoken text says 'neither he nor she' for neuter to keep it plain.

Puzzle shape: the odd detail is the it/he shift. 'Some hear the nots as the way to say what no picture can hold, and the poet as the same reality turned toward us' is one hedged reading; confirm it is fair and add another school's reading if a Keeper prefers.
Grammar to confirm: sa paryagat ('he has gone around'); kaya, vrana, snava, viddha glosses. The gloss 'Kavir' with Devanagari कविर् shows the sandhi form before manishi; confirm or simplify.
'A short a at the front can mean not' is stated as 'can', not 'always'. howItsDone's 'two ways of speaking' (neti neti and positive description) is general; confirm wording.
